title: Ancient Galaxy Collision Transformed the Milky Way Billions of Years Ago, Studies Reveal
excerpt: New research shows the Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus merger 11 billion years ago destroyed and rebuilt the Milky Way's disk, triggering an explosion of star formation.
body:
• A study in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society shows that the Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus merger likely occurred about 11 billion years ago, earlier than many previous estimates.
  • The collision partially or completely destroyed the Milky Way's spinning stellar disk, which then had to rebuild from scratch — reshaping the galaxy we see today.
  • The research also reveals that the Milky Way is currently being pulled into a new collision with the Large Magellanic Cloud, its most massive companion galaxy.

The Milky Way's apparent calm is a cosmic illusion. Beneath the serene band of stars visible on a clear night lies a violent history of galactic collisions, and new research is piecing together exactly how one ancient encounter reshaped our home galaxy from the inside out.

A study published in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society by researchers at the University of Barcelona's Institute of Cosmos Sciences and the Institute of Space Studies of Catalonia uses advanced simulations to show that the Milky Way's rotating stellar disk — the vast, pancake-shaped structure containing most of its stars, including our sun — was likely destroyed and rebuilt after a cataclysmic merger roughly 11 billion years ago.

The Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus Merger

The collision in question involved a massive dwarf galaxy now known as Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus (GSE), whose existence was confirmed in 2018 using data from the European Space Agency's Gaia mission. The name "sausage" refers to a distinctive elongated pattern in the motions of its remnant stars.

https://x.com/esa/status/2089394354276184373

Previous estimates placed this merger at around 8 to 10 billion years ago, but the new simulations push the timeline back further, to approximately 11 billion years. That revised timing coincides with a sharp increase in the formation of star clusters in the Milky Way — a "galactic firework" triggered by the collision compressing gas and sparking intense star formation.

"Models of the Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus merger predict that a galactic firework should have followed the impact. This is the first time this link has been made."

— Chervin F. P. Laporte, researcher, French National Centre for Scientific Research

Reading the Fossil Record of Stars

The research builds on decades of galactic archaeology — a field that uses the ages, chemical compositions and orbits of stars as fossils to reconstruct the Milky Way's past. Migrant stars, those not born in our galaxy, cut across the orderly rotation of native stars, plunging into the inner galaxy and flying back out in distinctive patterns.

These migrant stars tend to be less enriched in heavier elements, a chemical signature of slower evolution typical of smaller dwarf galaxies. By tracing their paths, scientists can identify the remnants of galaxies the Milky Way consumed over billions of years.

The GSE merger was not the only major collision in the Milky Way's history. Earlier research identified at least five major mergers involving galaxies with more than 100 million stars each, stretching back 6 to 11 billion years. The so-called Kraken merger, identified through globular cluster analysis, may have been even more transformative given the Milky Way's smaller size at the time.

A New Collision Ahead

The Milky Way's period of relative calm is ending. The Large Magellanic Cloud, currently the galaxy's most massive companion, is already pulling at the Milky Way and disturbing its dark matter halo. Scientists say this gravitational dance will ultimately result in another merger — echoing the destruction and rebirth the galaxy experienced billions of years ago.

Tools like the James Webb Space Telescope and the Atacama Large Millimeter Array are now enabling scientists to observe similar galaxy formation processes in the distant universe, providing a window into what the Milky Way may have looked like during its violent youth.

"The calm band of light above us is not a symbol of permanence, but a visible reminder of a long survival."

— Vasily Belokurov, 2026 Kavli Prize winner in Astrophysics
